_about.what: The numbers of a fleet action fought out on the field (src/battle/sea). Every ship's weight, toughness and nation's quality come from data/campaign/navy.json, as the rules count them: this file only says how the field plays them out. Abstract by design (project memory air-battle-paused, ruling 217): pieces wear each other down within reach, by the angle their guns bear; nothing is aimed and nothing flies.
_about.field: The sea is a square of 'size' metres. The attacker's fleets come on from the south edge, 'edge' metres in, the defender's from the north, in rows 'row' metres apart: destroyers ahead, then cruisers, battleships and carriers. 'limit' is the battle time in seconds before it is called on the exchange so far.
_about.classes: speed in metres a second at cruising speed (the historian's: battleships 11, cruisers 13, destroyers 14, carriers 13); turn in radians a second at full way (a ship turns slower when slow, and barely at all when stopped); reach is the furthest its guns hit at all (the one ring the screens draw) and a ship nearer the enemy than three quarters of best turns away to open the range; per is how many ships of the class sail as one piece (destroyers in fours); crew is a ship's company, for the after-action card only; len and beam are a ship's length and breadth in metres, for the screens and the 3D models; a piece's ships sail in line ahead, three lengths apart. Battleships, cruisers and destroyers have one reach and hit with one punch for each unit of their weight (the design director, b415): the campaign's card already prices a battleship as more weight than a cruiser, so the field does not count the class a second time. Classes differ in speed, turning, toughness and their place in the line, and their salvos differ in look only (battleships slow and heavy, destroyers quick and light: SALVO in src/battle/ui/sea-draw.ts), with the same harm per unit of weight each minute. A carrier fights by its strike, not its guns: standoff is how far it keeps from the nearest enemy, behind its own screen and beyond the guns' reach.
_about.speeds: Shares of a class's cruising speed for the speed order, and accel, how fast way is gained or lost (metres a second, each second).
_about.fire: rate turns weight into wear on a hull each second, the same for every class. hull: a side's hulls together come to this many times its weight, shared over its ships by the rules' toughness (a battleship takes about twice the wear of its weight that a destroyer does); every shot, strike and raid takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it falls on, so toughness decides which ships go down and not who wins. far is what a piece does at the edge of its reach against 1 at its best range or closer: 1, so guns tell as hard anywhere in reach, and a ship in the rear rows is not worth less than its weight for standing further back (at 0.5, a fleet strong in the ships behind the line won 10 points less than the card). endOn is what its guns do when the target is dead ahead or astern, against 1 on the beam: crossing the T. damaged: a crippled ship still fights at this share. retarget: seconds between a piece looking for a new target.
_about.nerve: A piece's nerve falls by 'hit' for each whole hull it takes in wear, and when a ship of its own side goes down within 'nearR' metres by 'near' times that ship's share of its side's weight (a cruiser lost from a fleet of weight 60 shakes it by 0.06, a destroyer by 0.02, a battleship by 0.2: the design director, b438), so a fleet of many light ships is shaken no more for the same weight lost; out of the fight for 'quiet' seconds it mends at 'mend' a second. Below 'waver' it wavers and fights at 'wavering'; below 'break' it breaks off for its own edge.
_about.side: A side breaks off when it has lost 'breakAt' of its strength as the card counts it, its ships and its coasts' aircraft together (a share of 'spread' either way, more with a good admiral: 'admiral' a level). After a side breaks, its enemy has 'pursuit' seconds to make it pay before the battle ends. The luck of the day is the rules' own: one roll of the dice's run (0.8 to 1.2, navy.ts seaBattles) for the battle, the attacker's ships fighting that much better and the defender's that much worse, so that with nobody playing the field gives what the dice give. Once the enemy has broken off, every ship of the side still fighting runs it down at full speed, the player's as the staff's, until the player gives an order of their own (b402).
_about.strike: A carrier's strike: ordered, it is flown within the second and lands 'windup' seconds later on the target and the ships near it within 'radius', and the carrier can strike again 'every' seconds after that. A strike carries the weight of 'every' seconds of the carrier's own weight at 'share', its own weight being what is left of its air group. It takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it falls on (wear in proportion to the ship's hull), so the screen is no cheaper a target than the battleship. Every blow on a side, by gun, strike or raid, wears the whole of what the side brought by weight: the ship it fell on for the gun ships' share, each carrier for its own (as a hull wears, but out of its air group: it stays afloat) and the coasts' aircraft for theirs (b415). Kept whole at 6,000 m while the gun ships wore, carriers were worth more the longer the gun fight ran, a tenth or more of the card either way with the fleets' make-up; worn with their fleet, share 0.34 keeps them within the dice attacking and attacked, with a light screen or a mixed one. Carriers with no gun ship at all are not: the field cannot honour an action where one side has none, so the staff settles it and the field is not offered it (the design director, b438: carriers against carriers is an air battle, and the field flies no planes). With no strike ordered a carrier strikes its fleet's common target. It is counted, not flown: no aircraft are on the field.
_about.air: Aircraft from the coasts (the rules' airOver, times navy.json air.weight) raid every 'every' seconds, the first within the first raid's span; each raid's weight is 'share' of what that much weight of guns would deal in the time, as a strike's is, and like gunfire it takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it finds. The card counts the coasts' aircraft in a side's strength, so the field does: they are worn by every blow on their side by their share of its weight, and having no hull they lose the whole of it, where a ship's hull takes it at 'fire.hull' (b415). Each raid is as strong as the aircraft left. Share 0.5 keeps the coasts' aircraft within the dice on either side, from a few against a fleet to most of a side's strength.
_about.pieces: No more than 'most' pieces a side: past that, cruisers sail in twos, then destroyers in more than fours.
_about.ai: The computer's captains (and the player's, where no order is given): each side fires on one common target, the enemy piece nearest the middle of its own fleet, kept until it goes or breaks off, when the enemy then nearest the middle that is still fighting takes its place; a ship that cannot reach it fires on another in reach. That is exactly what a newcomer does (select all, right-click the enemy nearest the middle, Space), so the newcomer's battle and the staff's are the same (b402). A ship further than 'keep' metres from the middle of its own fleet works back toward it as it fights. A ship steers for the enemy nearest it, and for its target only when that lies more than 'beyond' metres further off than the nearest enemy (ruling 226, 4: every ship sent at one point made a knot the enemy fought around). Until the guns first meet, a fleet keeps together: its gun ships sail at the speed of its slowest gun ship, and one more than 'station' metres ahead of the rearmost of them slows to half that speed until the line comes up, so the screen closes up on the battle line and stays just ahead of it (the historian: fleet speed was the slowest heavy ship's, and the screen kept station on the battle line). Drawn up 700 m a row apart and each at its own speed, a battle line reached the fight a minute after its screen and lost to a light fleet of the same weight 95 times in 100; with the screen kept 600 m ahead it still came 13 in 100 short (b407, ruling 217). A fleet keeps together only to meet a gun line: not once either side has broken off (the chase runs at full speed) and not against an enemy with no gun ship left: then every gun ship not sent at a speed of its own runs the carriers down at full speed, as a broken enemy is. A ship the player sends at a speed of their own, or on a course, goes as told. A ship within 'broadside' metres of the enemy it is steering for turns to bring its broadside to bear; further off it closes. Closing until 3,450 m left the ships behind their own screen end-on for the whole fight.
_about.evade: A carrier group without battleships that sees an enemy battleship within 'see' metres of a carrier turns away from it and opens the range at 'speed' times a carrier's cruising speed, launching as it goes, unless the player has ordered it to steer, hold or withdraw (a carrier evades even when ordered to strike). Near the edge of the field it turns along it. 'screen' is how near a carrier a ship of its screen must be to turn away with it: 0, so the screen stays and fights (b402: a screen that ran with its carriers left the plain order short of the card). A fleet with battleships of its own stands and fights, its carriers behind the line.
